title: DOL starter: wire, start and fault-find
summary: Wire a direct-on-line starter with 24 V DC control, prove it works, then find hidden faults by measuring.

why.text:
Conveyor **CV-3** at the fictional Riverside bottling plant has a new 2.2 kW motor. It needs a starter: press START and it runs, press STOP and it stops, and if the motor is overloaded it must trip and **stay off** until someone deals with it.

The direct-on-line (DOL) starter does exactly this. It is the most common starter you will meet. Faster faults get found by technicians who understand **why** each wire is there.

cards.title: What a DOL starter does
cards.text:
[[DOL]] means the motor is switched straight onto the full 400 V supply. It is simple and cheap, and gives full starting torque.

The catch: while starting, the motor draws several times its [[FLC]] (often 6 to 8 times) for a second or two. That is fine for small motors. Large motors use star-delta, soft starters or drives instead (later lessons).

cards.title: The power circuit
cards.text:
Follow the three phases from top to bottom:
1. **Q1** [[MPCB]]: protects against short circuits and lets you switch the circuit off.
2. **KM1** [[contactor]] main poles: open and close to start and stop the motor.
3. **F2** [[overload relay]]: measures motor current, and trips if it is too high for too long.
4. **M1** motor terminals U1, V1, W1, plus the earth (PE).

The phase order at U1, V1, W1 sets the direction. Swapping **any two** phases reverses the motor.

cards.title: 24 V DC control
cards.text:
The control circuit runs at 24 V DC from power supply **G1**, fed through MCB **F1**. Low voltage control is safer for people operating push buttons, and it matches PLC inputs and outputs.

Notice G1 is fed from **after** Q1: switching Q1 off kills the control circuit too.

cards.title: The holding (latch) contact
cards.text:
START (S2) is a push button with a [[NO]] contact. It only closes while you press it. So how does the motor keep running when you let go?

KM1 has an auxiliary NO contact, **13-14**, wired **in parallel** with START. When the coil pulls in, 13-14 closes and keeps feeding the coil after you release START. This is the [[holding contact]].

cards.title: Why STOP is normally closed
cards.text:
STOP (S1) is a [[NC]] contact, wired in **series** with everything else. Pressing it breaks the coil circuit and the contactor drops out.

If a STOP wire breaks or comes loose, the coil circuit opens and the motor stops. A fault makes the motor **stop**, never **fail to stop**. We call this fail-safe.

The overload's NC contact **95-96** sits in the same series path, so an overload trip also drops out KM1.

cards.title: Overload protection, and no automatic restart
cards.text:
Set the overload to the motor's **nameplate full-load current**. Here that is 4.6 A.

When it trips, 95-96 opens and KM1 drops out. Contact **97-98** closes and lights the TRIP lamp H2.

Resetting the overload must **not** restart the motor. Because the holding contact opened when KM1 dropped out, someone has to press START again. A motor that restarts by itself can injure a person who is clearing a jam.

show.intro: This starter is wired correctly and switched on. Work through each task. The event log explains what happens and why.

tasks.text: Press and hold START (S2). KM1 pulls in and the motor starts.
Let go of START. The motor keeps running because KM1 13-14 now feeds the coil.
Measure the voltage across the coil KM1 A1 to A2 with the meter in V= mode.
Press STOP (S1). KM1 drops out and the motor coasts to a stop.
Start the motor again, then press TEST on the overload F2. The motor stops and TRIP lamp H2 lights.
Press RESET on F2. The motor does NOT restart by itself. Now press START to run it again.

guided.intro: The power circuit and lamps are already wired. **Wire the control circuit**: STOP, START, the holding contact, the overload contact and the coil. Tap a terminal, then tap another to add a wire. Tap a wire to select it and delete it.
hints: Start at G1 + (24 V). It feeds STOP S1 terminal 11.
From S1 terminal 12, go to START S2 terminal 13.
The holding contact KM1 13-14 goes in parallel with S2: wire S2:13 to KM1:13 and S2:14 to KM1:14.
After S2:14, go through the overload contact F2 95-96 (it is closed when not tripped).
F2:96 feeds the coil KM1:A1. KM1:A2 returns to G1 − (0 V).

unguided.intro: Now wire the **power circuit from Q1 to the motor** and the **whole control circuit**, with no hints. The supply, control supply and lamps are already wired.

checks.fail: There is a short circuit: a protective device tripped as soon as power was applied. Look for a wire joining two different supply conductors.
The circuit will not settle (relay chatter). Check that the coil is not switching its own supply off.
The 24 V supply G1 is off. Check the feed from Q1 through F1 to G1.
KM1 pulls in without anyone pressing START. Check that START is a normally open contact and the holding contact is not bridging it permanently.
The motor runs before KM1 is switched on. The power circuit must pass through the KM1 main poles.
Pressing START does not pull in KM1. Trace the path from G1 + through S1, S2 and F2 95-96 to KM1 A1, and from A2 back to G1 −.
KM1 drops out when you let go of START. The holding contact KM1 13-14 must be wired in parallel with START.
KM1 is on but the motor is not running on three phases. Trace each phase Q1 → KM1 → F2 → M1.
The motor runs backwards. Connect F2:2 to U1, F2:4 to V1 and F2:6 to W1 (or swap two phases).
The motor is not fed through the overload F2 power poles, so it is not protected.
The RUN lamp H1 is not lit while the motor runs.
Pressing STOP does not drop out KM1. STOP must be a normally closed contact in series with the coil circuit.
The motor restarts when STOP is released. The holding contact must sit after STOP, not around it.
With STOP and START pressed together, the motor runs. STOP must always win: put STOP before START in the series path.
An overload trip does not stop the motor. The F2 95-96 contact must be in series with the coil.
The TRIP lamp H2 does not light when F2 trips.
The motor restarts by itself when the overload is reset. This is dangerous. The holding contact must be the only thing keeping the coil on after START.

break.intro: This starter has **one hidden fault**. Operate it to see the symptom, then use the meter to find the cause. In this simulator you may measure voltage with the power on. On a real panel, live testing is only allowed when it is justified, by a competent person, following the site risk assessment and GS38. Switch off Q1 before any resistance (Ω) test. When you know the cause, choose it from the list.

faults.report: Overload contact F2 95-96 is open, although the overload has not tripped.
Holding contact KM1 13-14 does not close.
The KM1 coil is open circuit (burnt out).
Q1 pole 5-6 is open: phase L3 does not reach the motor.
The wire from KM1 A2 to G1 0 V is broken.
The wire from S1 terminal 12 to S2 terminal 13 is broken.

extraReports: Nothing is wrong with the starter.

questions.text: In a DOL starter, what keeps the contactor energised after START is released?
options: The holding contact KM1 13-14 wired in parallel with START
questions.explain: The auxiliary NO contact closes when the coil pulls in and bridges START.

questions.text: Why is a STOP button wired with a normally closed contact?
options: So a broken wire or loose terminal stops the motor (fail-safe)
questions.explain: With NC in series, any break in the stop circuit stops the motor instead of leaving it unable to stop.

questions.text: The overload trips. You find the cause and reset the overload. What should the motor do?
options: Stay stopped until someone presses START
questions.explain: An automatic restart could injure someone working on the machine. Resetting must never restart the motor.

questions.text: What does the thermal overload relay protect against?
options: The motor overheating from too much current for too long
questions.explain: Short circuits are cleared by the MPCB or fuses. Shock protection is by earthing and RCDs. The overload protects the motor.

questions.text: A motor nameplate shows a full-load current of 4.6 A. Where do you set the overload?
options: Half of 4.6 A for extra safety
questions.explain: Set it to the nameplate FLC. The overload's time delay already allows for the short starting current.

questions.text: A 4-pole motor on a 50 Hz supply has a synchronous speed of:
questions.explain: n = 120 × f ÷ poles = 120 × 50 ÷ 4 = 1500 rpm. The real speed is a little lower (slip), for example 1430 rpm.

questions.text: The motor runs the wrong way. What is the fix?
options: Isolate, prove dead, then swap any two phases at the motor
Swap the START and STOP wires
Reverse the 24 V supply to the coil
Swap the PE and one phase
questions.explain: Swapping any two phases reverses rotation. PE must never be swapped with a phase.

questions.text: The motor hums but does not turn, and the overload trips after a few seconds. What is the most likely cause?
options: The 24 V supply is too high
questions.explain: On two phases a stopped motor cannot start. It draws high current until the overload trips.

questions.text: Before changing any wiring in the starter, you must:
options: Isolate, lock off and prove dead
Tell the operator you are working on it
questions.explain: STOP and control MCBs are not isolation. Safe isolation is needed before any wiring work.

questions.text: With START pressed, you measure 24 V DC across KM1 A1–A2 but the contactor does not pull in. What is the most likely fault?
questions.explain: Full voltage across the coil but no pull-in points to the coil itself. A broken feed or return would show 0 V across it.

apply.intro: Do this on the training bench while your trainer watches. Your trainer signs it off. An app score alone never makes anyone competent or authorised.

items.text: Carries out safe isolation before starting work.
Wires the power and control circuits to the drawing: correct terminations, ferrules where used, tidy routing and labels.
Sets the overload to the motor nameplate full-load current.
Before energising, carries out and records continuity and insulation resistance tests to the site procedure.
Functional test with the trainer: start, latch, stop, overload trip, no automatic restart after reset, correct direction.
Leaves the panel safe: covers fitted, tools removed, isolation removed following the procedure.
